claim: Women made up only 25% of participants in landmark trials for congestive heart failure.
source: For example, women made up only 25% of participants in landmark trials for congestive heart failure and 19.2% of participants for studies in antiretroviral treatment of HIV (Criado-Perez, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Criado-Perez, 2019.

claim: Women made up 19.2% of participants for studies in antiretroviral treatment of HIV.
source: For example, women made up only 25% of participants in landmark trials for congestive heart failure and 19.2% of participants for studies in antiretroviral treatment of HIV (Criado-Perez, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Criado-Perez, 2019.

claim: Circadian timing is phase-advanced (earlier) in female compared to male individuals, as seen in the core body temperature minimum and evening rise in melatonin.
source: for instance, circadian timing is phase-advanced (earlier) in female compared to male individuals, as seen in the core body temperature minimum and evening rise in melatonin (Boivin et al., 2016; Cain et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boivin et al., 2016 and Cain et al., 2010.

claim: Female individuals have a shorter circadian period of the temperature and melatonin rhythms.
source: Female individuals also have a shorter circadian period of the temperature and melatonin rhythms (Duffy et al., 2011), and larger amplitude of the melatonin rhythm (Cain et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duffy et al., 2011.

claim: Female individuals have larger amplitude of the melatonin rhythm.
source: Female individuals also have a shorter circadian period of the temperature and melatonin rhythms (Duffy et al., 2011), and larger amplitude of the melatonin rhythm (Cain et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cain et al., 2010.

claim: More male individuals are late chronotypes than females.
source: Furthermore, sex differences exist in chronotype, the circadian continuum of early ('larks') to late ('owls') diurnal preference (Chontong et al., 2016), such that more male individuals are late types than females (Fischer et al., 2017; Roenneberg et al., 2004; Fischer et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2017; Roenneberg et al., 2004; Fischer et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2017.

claim: Female individuals have an earlier timing of sleep, longer sleep duration and more slow-wave sleep.
source: With regard to sleep, female individuals have an earlier timing of sleep, longer sleep duration and more slow-wave sleep (Roenneberg et al., 2004; Dijk et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roenneberg et al., 2004 and Dijk et al., 1989.

claim: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease (Yoon et al., 2014), inflammation (Okun et al., 2011), metabolic disorders (Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011), mental health conditions (Lemola et al., 2013; Vanderlind et al., 2014), and cognitive impairment (McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoon et al., 2014.

claim: Irregular sleep is associated with inflammation.
source: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease (Yoon et al., 2014), inflammation (Okun et al., 2011), metabolic disorders (Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011), mental health conditions (Lemola et al., 2013; Vanderlind et al., 2014), and cognitive impairment (McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Okun et al., 2011.

claim: Irregular sleep is associated with metabolic disorders.
source: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease (Yoon et al., 2014), inflammation (Okun et al., 2011), metabolic disorders (Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011), mental health conditions (Lemola et al., 2013; Vanderlind et al., 2014), and cognitive impairment (McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011.

claim: Irregular sleep is associated with mental health conditions.
source: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease (Yoon et al., 2014), inflammation (Okun et al., 2011), metabolic disorders (Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011), mental health conditions (Lemola et al., 2013; Vanderlind et al., 2014), and cognitive impairment (McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lemola et al., 2013 and Vanderlind et al., 2014.

claim: Irregular sleep is associated with cognitive impairment.
source: Irregular sleep is associated with cardiovascular disease (Yoon et al., 2014), inflammation (Okun et al., 2011), metabolic disorders (Patel et al., 2014; Chontong et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2011), mental health conditions (Lemola et al., 2013; Vanderlind et al., 2014), and cognitive impairment (McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McBean and Montgomery-Downs, 2013.

claim: 'Owls' tend to be more irregular sleepers.
source: Chronotype may account for these inconsistencies as 'owls' tend to be more irregular sleepers (Duffy et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duffy et al., 2011 and Fischer et al., 2017.

claim: More male individuals were found to be irregular sleepers than females when both were a later chronotype.
source: Indeed, in revisiting three published datasets (Fischer et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2017), more male individuals were found to be irregular sleepers than females when both were a later chronotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three datasets: Fischer et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2017.

claim: Variability in sleep duration was significantly associated with weight gain in male but not female students.
source: To the best of our knowledge, only one study examined this question (Roane et al., 2015), finding that variability in sleep duration was significantly associated with weight gain in male but not female students.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roane et al., 2015.

claim: Shift workers account for about a third of the workforce in North America and Europe.
source: Shift workers (approximately 50% of which are women) account for about a third of the workforce in North America and Europe, (Kervezee et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kervezee et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately 50% of shift workers are women.
source: Shift workers (approximately 50% of which are women) account for about a third of the workforce in North America and Europe, (Kervezee et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kervezee et al., 2018.

claim: Women have higher injury rates during night work than men.
source: Women have higher injury rates during night work than men, despite the injury rates between men and women being similar in day workers (Safe Work Australia, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Safe Work Australia, 2009.

claim: Injury rates between men and women are similar in day workers.
source: Women have higher injury rates during night work than men, despite the injury rates between men and women being similar in day workers (Safe Work Australia, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Safe Work Australia, 2009.

claim: Women in the follicular phase of their menstrual cycle had more sleep loss-related alertness failure than men.
source: This work showed that women in the follicular phase of their menstrual cycle had more sleep loss-related alertness failure than men, whereas there were no differences between women in the luteal phase and men (Vidafar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vidafar et al., 2018.

claim: There were no differences in sleep loss-related alertness failure between women in the luteal phase and men.
source: This work showed that women in the follicular phase of their menstrual cycle had more sleep loss-related alertness failure than men, whereas there were no differences between women in the luteal phase and men (Vidafar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vidafar et al., 2018.

claim: Female patients are more susceptible than their male counterparts to the side effects of widely used anticancer drugs.
source: Female patients are more susceptible than their male counterparts to the side effects of widely used anticancer drugs (Milano et al., 1992; Stein et al., 1995; Chansky et al., 2005; Cristina et al., 2018), and they can experience more frequent and severe toxicities from chemotherapy protocols due to sex differences in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (Gandhi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Milano et al., 1992; Stein et al., 1995; Chansky et al., 2005; Cristina et al., 2018.

claim: Female patients can experience more frequent and severe toxicities from chemotherapy protocols due to sex differences in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.
source: Female patients are more susceptible than their male counterparts to the side effects of widely used anticancer drugs (Milano et al., 1992; Stein et al., 1995; Chansky et al., 2005; Cristina et al., 2018), and they can experience more frequent and severe toxicities from chemotherapy protocols due to sex differences in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (Gandhi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gandhi et al., 2004.

claim: The molecular circadian clock rhythmically controls drug bioactivation, detoxification and transport.
source: Across the 24 hour cycle, the molecular circadian clock rhythmically controls drug bioactivation, detoxification and transport while the circadian timing system as a whole regulates drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (Dallmann et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dallmann et al., 2016.

claim: The circadian timing system as a whole regulates drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
source: Across the 24 hour cycle, the molecular circadian clock rhythmically controls drug bioactivation, detoxification and transport while the circadian timing system as a whole regulates drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (Dallmann et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dallmann et al., 2016.

claim: Timing is a critical factor in the tolerability and efficacy of over 50 anticancer medications in experimental models.
source: In experimental models, this results in strong circadian changes in the tolerability and efficacy of over 50 anticancer medications, indicating that timing is a critical factor (Dallmann et al., 2016; Lévi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dallmann et al., 2016 and Lévi et al., 2010.

claim: The intravenous delivery of the drug 5-FU leucovorin (5-FU-LV) at a constant rate resulted in circadian changes in drug concentration in plasma.
source: For instance, a study examining colorectal cancer – the third cause of cancer deaths worldwide – showed that the intravenous delivery of the drug 5-FU leucovorin (5-FU-LV) at a constant rate resulted in circadian changes in drug concentration in plasma (Petit et al., 1988; Fustin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Petit et al., 1988 and Fustin et al., 2012.

claim: Female patients had reduced 24 hour mean and circadian amplitude of the 5-FU body clearance compared to their male counterparts.
source: Most importantly, female patients had reduced 24 hour mean and circadian amplitude of the 5-FU body clearance compared to their male counterparts (Bressolle et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bressolle et al., 1999.

claim: Peak delivery at 1pm or 4pm for oxaliplatin and at 1am or 4am for 5-FU-LV proved to be least toxic by up to six-fold in male patients.
source: Furthermore, peak delivery at 1pm or 4pm for oxaliplatin (another anticancer drug) and at 1am or 4am for 5-FU-LV proved to be least toxic by up to six-fold in male patients, whilst optimal timing was located six hours later in female patients (Lévi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lévi et al., 2007.

claim: Optimal drug timing for oxaliplatin and 5-FU-LV was located six hours later in female patients compared to male patients.
source: Furthermore, peak delivery at 1pm or 4pm for oxaliplatin (another anticancer drug) and at 1am or 4am for 5-FU-LV proved to be least toxic by up to six-fold in male patients, whilst optimal timing was located six hours later in female patients (Lévi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lévi et al., 2007.

claim: The sex data gap exists in in vivo research.
source: The sex data gap exists both in in vivo (Curtis et al., 2018) and in vitro research (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2020) and is apparent even in diseases that predominantly affect women (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Curtis et al., 2018.

claim: The sex data gap exists in in vitro research.
source: The sex data gap exists both in in vivo (Curtis et al., 2018) and in vitro research (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2020) and is apparent even in diseases that predominantly affect women (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2020.

claim: The sex data gap is apparent even in diseases that predominantly affect women.
source: The sex data gap exists both in in vivo (Curtis et al., 2018) and in vitro research (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2020) and is apparent even in diseases that predominantly affect women (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2014.

claim: Researchers frequently ignore sex as a factor in the analysis, even when males and females are included in the study.
source: Critically, the sex gap is not just restricted to inclusion at the experimental design stage: researchers frequently ignore sex as a factor in the analysis, even when males and females are included in the study (Karp and Reavey, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karp and Reavey, 2019.

claim: A preliminary literature search on non-visual effects of light identified 545 papers.
source: A preliminary literature search identified 545 papers, which were evaluated against a list of exclusion criteria (see Methods for full details), yielding a total of 180 articles.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the literature search conducted by the authors.

claim: After applying exclusion criteria, 180 articles on non-visual effects of light were included in the analysis.
source: A preliminary literature search identified 545 papers, which were evaluated against a list of exclusion criteria (see Methods for full details), yielding a total of 180 articles.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the literature search conducted by the authors.

claim: 14 papers (7.77%) did not give sufficient information on the sex breakdown of participants.
source: Of the papers assessed, 14 (7.77%) did not give sufficient information on the sex breakdown of participants for this to be determined.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the analysis of 180 articles.

claim: In 166 articles on non-visual effects of light, females comprised an average of 33.9% of the sample.
source: In the remaining 166 articles, females comprised an average of 33.9% of the sample.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the analysis of 166 articles.

claim: Seven papers reported studying exclusively female participants.
source: Seven papers reported studying exclusively female participants, while 56 papers reported studying only males.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the analysis of articles.

claim: 56 papers reported studying only male participants.
source: Seven papers reported studying exclusively female participants, while 56 papers reported studying only males.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the analysis of articles.

claim: A large proportion of studies on non-visual effects of light used only male volunteers.
source: We conducted binomial tests to investigate the possibility of deviations from a balanced distribution of sexes, finding a large proportion of studies using only male volunteers.
evidence: The claim is based on binomial tests conducted on the data and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: Of 63 studies that exclusively involved male or female participants, only eleven (17.5%) provided text to justify this sample choice.
source: Next, we examined studies that exclusively involved male or female participants (N = 63). Of these, only eleven (17.5%) provided text to justify this sample choice.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the analysis of 63 studies.

claim: Publication year and proportion of female participants are correlated (r(164)=0.17, P = 0.02895).
source: We found some evidence that the number of females increased over time, with publication year and proportion of female participants being correlated (r(164)=0.17, P = 0.02895).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Total sample size correlates with the fraction of female participants in a given study (r(164)=0.3, P = 0.00008).
source: Interestingly, the total sample size correlates with the fraction of female participants in a given study (r(164)=0.3, P = 0.00008; Spearman's correlation): larger studies seem to recruit more balanced samples.
evidence: The claim is based on Spearman's correlation analysis of the data.

claim: Larger studies seem to recruit more balanced samples in terms of sex.
source: Interestingly, the total sample size correlates with the fraction of female participants in a given study (r(164)=0.3, P = 0.00008; Spearman's correlation): larger studies seem to recruit more balanced samples.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between sample size and proportion of female participants.

claim: A recent meta-analysis looking at 9,932 traits found that the variability seen in female mice was not greater than for male mice.
source: A recent meta-analysis looking at 9,932 traits found that the variability seen in female mice was not greater than for male mice – and in some cases was less – yet the legacy remains (Prendergast et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prendergast et al., 2014.

claim: In some cases, variability in female mice was less than in male mice.
source: A recent meta-analysis looking at 9,932 traits found that the variability seen in female mice was not greater than for male mice – and in some cases was less – yet the legacy remains (Prendergast et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prendergast et al., 2014.

claim: Biologically, crossed effects (where treatment effect goes in opposite direction for the sexes) are rare.
source: Biologically, crossed effects are rare, as shown in a large study assessing the prevalence of sexual dimorphism (Karp et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karp et al., 2017.

claim: A total of 275 participants registered for the entire workshop series.
source: A total of 275 participants registered for the entire workshop.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the workshop registration.

claim: Across the three workshops, between 38 and 94 attendees participated in the interactive sessions.
source: Across the three workshops, between 38 and 94 attendees participated in the interactive sessions, with approximately four out of five participants being researchers (82 out of 94 in Workshop 1, 47 out of 60 in Workshop 2 and 31 out of 38 in Workshop 3).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the workshop attendance.

claim: Approximately four out of five workshop participants were researchers.
source: Across the three workshops, between 38 and 94 attendees participated in the interactive sessions, with approximately four out of five participants being researchers (82 out of 94 in Workshop 1, 47 out of 60 in Workshop 2 and 31 out of 38 in Workshop 3).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the workshop attendance.

claim: Only 58% of workshop respondents (out of 100) indicated previously analyzing data in a sex-disaggregated fashion.
source: In an interactive polling segment following this workshop, only 58% of respondents (out of 100) indicated previously analyzing data in a sex-disaggregated fashion.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 1.

claim: 88.1% of workshop respondents (out of 101) agreed that sex could be a variable in their research.
source: However, 88.1% (out of 101) agreed that sex could be a variable in their research, showing the large scope for sex-disaggregated analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 1.

claim: Workshop participants indicated that their research could mostly influence precision and personalized medicine, occupational timing and shift/rota planning, and guidelines for an indoor 'circadian' lighting.
source: In the interactive polling segment following this workshop, participants indicated that their research could mostly influence precision and personalized medicine, occupational timing and shift/rota planning, and guidelines for an indoor 'circadian' lighting.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 2.

claim: Research money or funding and time were the most mentioned barriers to addressing sex bias in research by workshop participants.
source: When asked to identify the biggest barriers to addressing sex bias in research, research money or funding and time were the most mentioned factors, followed by guidelines and policies.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 2.

claim: Workshop participants first mentioned research institutes and universities as sources for guidance on sex-difference analysis.
source: In the interactive polling segment, when asked to rank sources for guidance on sex-difference analysis, the participants first mentioned research institutes and universities, then societies and professional bodies and finally funders and publishers.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 3.

claim: The top three priorities for workshop participants regarding funders were: (1) provision of training and guidance to incorporate sex and gender analysis; (2) allocation of funding within regular grant mechanisms ringfenced for sex and gender analysis; and (3) more allocation of funds in regular research grants.
source: In further exploring the role of funders, the top three priorities for participants were: (1) provision of training and guidance to incorporate sex and gender analysis; (2) allocation of funding within regular grant mechanisms ringfenced for sex and gender analysis; and (3) simply more allocation of funds in regular research grants.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 3.

claim: Three actionable items emerged from workshop participants regarding what researchers could personally do: (1) inclusion of sex and gender analysis as a central step in research; (2) learning from peers and with examples; and (3) upskilling in the requisite statistical techniques.
source: When asked what researchers could personally do, three actionable items emerged: (1) inclusion of sex and gender analysis as a central step in research; (2) learning from peers and with examples; and (3) upskilling in the requisite statistical techniques.
evidence: The claim is based on polling data from Workshop 3.

claim: Light plays a critical role in regulating physiology and behaviour via its influence on the circadian system.
source: Apart from vision, light plays a critical role in regulating physiology and behaviour via its influence on the circadian system.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about light and circadian systems.

claim: Non-visual effects of light are mediated by a multi-component photoreceptor system consisting of rods, cones and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye.
source: These effects are mediated by a multi-component photoreceptor system consisting of rods, cones and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye that transmit information to the circadian clock via the retinohypothalamic tract.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the photoreceptor system.

claim: The photoreceptor system transmits information to the circadian clock via the retinohypothalamic tract.
source: These effects are mediated by a multi-component photoreceptor system consisting of rods, cones and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in the eye that transmit information to the circadian clock via the retinohypothalamic tract.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about neural pathways.

claim: Colorectal cancer is the third cause of cancer deaths worldwide.
source: For instance, a study examining colorectal cancer – the third cause of cancer deaths worldwide – showed that the intravenous delivery of the drug 5-FU leucovorin (5-FU-LV) at a constant rate resulted in circadian changes in drug concentration in plasma (Petit et al., 1988; Fustin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the context of discussing colorectal cancer.

claim: There is a sex data gap in the literature on the non-visual effects of light.
source: In summary, we find a sex data gap in the literature on the non-visual effects of light, which needs to be considered in current efforts to translate research findings in the 'real world'.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of 180 articles showing imbalanced sex representation.

claim: The sex data gap in non-visual effects of light research needs to be considered in current efforts to translate research findings in the 'real world'.
source: In summary, we find a sex data gap in the literature on the non-visual effects of light, which needs to be considered in current efforts to translate research findings in the 'real world'.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the identified sex data gap and its implications for translation.

claim: Studying both males and females does not require the sample size to be doubled.
source: A related misconception is that studying both males and females requires the sample size to be doubled. Indeed, the analysis is not conducted independently for each sex; rather a regression analysis is used to explore the variation in the outcome variable of interest after accounting for effect of sex.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical reasoning about regression analysis.

claim: Regression analysis accounts for the variance introduced by sex, and the sensitivity for a treatment effect is minimally impacted by the inclusion of two sexes.
source: As regression analysis does not pool the data, the variance introduced by sex is accounted for, and the sensitivity for a treatment effect is minimally impacted by the inclusion of two sexes.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical principles of regression analysis.

claim: If data is collected independently for the two sexes, it becomes impossible to determine whether differences in estimate emerge due to sample variation or because the effect depends on sex.
source: If data is collected independently for the two sexes, it becomes impossible to determine whether differences in estimate emerge due to sample variation or because the effect depends on sex.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical reasoning about experimental design.

claim: In biomedical research, the target population will be, on average, 50% male and 50% female.
source: In biomedical research, the target population will be, on average, 50% male and 50% female, and it is becoming clear that variations between male and female physiology extend beyond hormonal differences.
evidence: The claim is based on general demographic knowledge about human populations.

claim: Variations between male and female physiology extend beyond hormonal differences.
source: In biomedical research, the target population will be, on average, 50% male and 50% female, and it is becoming clear that variations between male and female physiology extend beyond hormonal differences.
evidence: The claim is based on emerging scientific understanding of sex differences.

claim: Sex should be the first variable to be included in biomedical research to significantly increase generalizability, except for cases such as the study of sex-specific conditions or phenomena.
source: Therefore, as a rule, sex should be the first variable to be included to significantly increase generalizability – except, as discussed in the NIH guidelines, for cases such as the study of sex-specific conditions or phenomena.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on reasoning about generalizability and NIH guidelines.

claim: There is very little to no research about intersex individuals within circadian physiology and sleep research.
source: Furthermore, we acknowledge that there is very little to no research about intersex individuals within circadian physiology and sleep research, constituting an important gap.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Addressing the research gap on intersex individuals may contribute to better granularity and understanding of sex-differentiated biological mechanisms and responses.
source: Addressing this gap may contribute to better granularity and understanding of sex-differentiated biological mechanisms and responses.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential benefits of future research.

claim: Sex differences in sleep and circadian physiology remain underresearched despite far-reaching health implications.
source: Overall, despite the far-reaching health implications, sex differences in sleep and circadian physiology remain underresearched.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the review of literature presented in the manuscript.

claim: The physiological mechanisms underlying the difference in injury rates between men and women during night work remain unclear, partly due to a lack of research on the female circadian system.
source: The physiological mechanisms underlying this difference remains unclear, partly due to a lack of research on the female circadian system.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of research identified.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of sex differences in optimal drug timing appear to involve sex differences in molecular clock function.
source: Thus, optimal drug timing and optimal drug doses can differ according to sex (Spitschan et al., 2020). While the underlying mechanisms appear to involve sex differences in molecular clock function, their links with chrono-pharmacological determinants prompt further investigation.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about mechanisms that require further investigation.

claim: The links between sex differences in molecular clock function and chrono-pharmacological determinants prompt further investigation.
source: While the underlying mechanisms appear to involve sex differences in molecular clock function, their links with chrono-pharmacological determinants prompt further investigation.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research based on current knowledge gaps.

claim: Closing the sex data gap will require solutions to be bespoke for each research community.
source: The problems that allow sex bias to emerge are multifaceted and closing the data gap will require solutions to be bespoke for each research community.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the multifaceted nature of the problem.

claim: Embracing practices to improve sex inclusivity should improve translational outcomes and scientific efficiency.
source: Embracing these new practices should improve translational outcomes and scientific efficiency, but this will require a two-pronged tactic that both strengthens forces for change and weakens barriers in the field (Karp and Reavey, 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the benefits of improved practices, supported by a citation.

claim: Improving sex inclusivity will require a two-pronged tactic that both strengthens forces for change and weakens barriers in the field.
source: Embracing these new practices should improve translational outcomes and scientific efficiency, but this will require a two-pronged tactic that both strengthens forces for change and weakens barriers in the field (Karp and Reavey, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karp and Reavey, 2019.

claim: There is a scope for funding agencies to specifically address researchers' need for funding to address sex bias.
source: This indicates a scope for funding agencies to specifically address researchers' need for funding, as well as an opportunity for institutions, funders, professional bodies, learned societies and journals to develop clear guidance (see Box 1 for an example of a journal implementing a specific policy; and Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on workshop participants identifying funding as a barrier.

claim: There is an opportunity for institutions, funders, professional bodies, learned societies and journals to develop clear guidance on addressing sex bias.
source: This indicates a scope for funding agencies to specifically address researchers' need for funding, as well as an opportunity for institutions, funders, professional bodies, learned societies and journals to develop clear guidance (see Box 1 for an example of a journal implementing a specific policy; and Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on workshop participants identifying guidelines and policies as barriers.
